lectures.title: Ventilation, Lung Mechanics, Gas Transport and ABGs
lectures.framing: How air gets in and out (compliance, surface tension), how much of it reaches gas exchange (dead space, V/Q), and how the result is measured — PFTs for the mechanics and the ABG for the gases. The organising idea: obstruction traps air (↓ FEV1/FVC, ↑ volumes); restriction shrinks the lung (normal/↑ ratio, ↓ volumes).
lectures.keypoints: FEV1/FVC < 0.7 = obstruction; static volumes then split hyperinflation (> 120%) from restriction (< 80%), and DLCO separates parenchymal (↓) from extraparenchymal (normal) restriction. Shunt (V/Q = 0) does NOT correct with 100% O2; dead space (V/Q = ∞, e.g. PE) does. Surfactant ↓ surface tension (Laplace ΔP = 2Υ/r) so small alveoli do not collapse. Right shift = ↓ affinity, ↑ unloading (↑ H+, temperature, PCO2, 2,3-BPG). CO2 travels mostly as bicarbonate (70%). The body never overcompensates; lungs compensate in minutes, kidneys in a day.

blocks.html:
Ventilation — moving air in and out of the lung

Inspiration — active; contraction of the inspiratory muscles

  • Diaphragm — phrenic nerves (C3-5); referred pain to shoulder and trapezius ridge
  • External intercostals — intercostal nerves
  • ↑ thoracic cavity volume → ↑ negative intrapleural pressure → lung expands → intrapulmonary pressure -1 mm Hg → air flows in

Expiration — passive; elastic recoil of lung and chest wall to their equilibrium positions

  • Becomes active during exercise and voluntary hyperventilation, using:
  • Abdominal wall muscles (rectus abdominis, internal and external obliques, transversus abdominis)
  • Internal intercostals

Compliance and surface tension

Pulmonary compliance = ΔV / ΔP; normal = 22 mL/cm H2O

  • ↑ compliance = lung easier to fill — emphysema, older adults
  • ↓ compliance = lung harder to fill — pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS

Pressure-volume (PV) curves — non-linear; lungs most compliant between 10-20 mm Hg

  • Hysteresis: inflation and deflation curves differ because of surface tension forces during inflation — ↑ volume during deflation
  • 1/3 of the pressure to fill the lung overcomes elastic forces; 2/3 overcomes surface tension at the air-liquid interface

Law of Laplace: ΔP = 2Υ / r (Υ = surface tension, r = radius)

  • Small lung volumes = small r = small Υ; large lung volumes = large r = large Υ
  • When surface tension is high, alveoli collapse easily, especially when the radius is small
  • Surfactant forms a lipid film at the air-liquid interface → ↓ surface tension → ↓ alveolar collapse, ↓ lung recoil, ↑ compliance

blocks.html:
Minute and alveolar ventilation
  • Minute ventilation (VE) — air entering the lungs per minute: VE = VT × RR; normal = 500 × 12 = 6000 mL
  • Alveolar ventilation (VA) — air entering the respiratory zone per minute:
    VA = (VT − VD) × RR
    VA = VE × (1 − VD/VT)
    VA = (VCO2 × 0.863) / PACO2
  • VA changes with changes in VT and RR even at the same minute ventilation
Physiologic dead space (VD) — inspired air that does NOT take part in gas exchange
  • Anatomic dead space + alveolar dead space; normal = 150 mL
  • Equals anatomic dead space in normal lungs; may be greater in lung disease with V/Q mismatch
  • The apex of healthy lungs is the largest contributor of alveolar dead space
  • Bohr equation: VD = VT × (PaCO2 − PECO2) / PaCO2, where PECO2 = expired air PCO2

Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q)
  • Ventilation (V) — gas going into the alveoli; perfusion (Q) — blood flow to the alveoli
  • Ideal V/Q = 1; normal V/Q = 0.8
  • V/Q = 0 — airway obstruction (shunt): V = 0, so 100% O2 does NOT improve PaO2
  • V/Q = ∞ — blood obstruction (physiological dead space): Q = 0, 100% O2 improves PaO2 — pulmonary embolism

blocks.title: Shunt vs dead space on 100% O2
blocks.html: Shunt (V/Q = 0) does not respond to supplemental O2 — the added oxygen never reaches the unventilated alveoli. Dead space (V/Q = ∞, e.g. PE) does improve.

blocks.html:
Pulmonary function tests

Spirometry measures lung volumes and function; body plethysmography (body box) is based on Boyle's law (P1V1 = P2V2)

  • Indications: diagnosis of dyspnea or cough NYD, prognosis and severity (obstructive, restrictive), monitoring treatment response
  • Contraindications: aneurysms (cerebral > thoracic, abdominal), pneumothorax, recent brain or eye surgery, severe hypertension (> 200/120), recent MI/arrhythmias, stress/strain syncope
  • Effort-dependent: maximal inspiration (FVC) and rapid expiration (FEV1) with prolonged expiratory effort; nose clipped
  • Standardized by age, sex, height and ethnicity
What is measured
  • FEV1 — fraction of VC expired in 1 second; normal = 80% VC
  • FVC — maximum volume forcibly exhaled after maximal inspiration
  • FEV1/FVC (Tiffeneau-Pinelli index) — defines obstructive lung disease
  • Static lung volumes: most people breathe at 50% (highest compliance); hyperinflation > 120% (↑ RV, gas trapping); restriction < 80% — parenchymal (lung) or extraparenchymal (diaphragm, chest wall, pleura)
  • Diffusion capacity (DLCO) — conductance of CO from inspired gas to RBCs (CO has a much higher affinity than O2)
DLCO details
  • KCO = DLCO/VA; normal > 75%
  • ↓ CO uptake = parenchymal pathology; ↓ perfusion, thickened membrane, ↑ volume, ↑ surface area
  • Isolated DLCO abnormalities: anemia (no RBCs to take up CO), pulmonary vascular disorders (PE, pulmonary hypertension), early ILD (not enough to cause restriction), non-obstructive emphysema, early pneumonia

blocks.html:
PFT interpretation — three steps
  1. Spirometry: FEV1/FVC ratio — look at the actual values
  2. Static lung volumes: hyperinflated (> 120%) or restricted (< 80%) — parenchymal or extraparenchymal
  3. Diffusion capacity: reduced or preserved — localizes the anatomical restriction

blocks.html:
Oxygen transport
  • Bound to Hb (major) — 4 subunits (2 α, 2 β), each heme binds 1 O2 (4 O2 total)
    • 1 g Hb = 1.34 mL O2; 15 g Hb/100 mL → 20.1 mL O2 bound to Hb
    • Oxygenated Hb: high affinity (relaxed configuration) — positive cooperativity
    • Deoxygenated Hb: low affinity (tense configuration)
    • Myoglobin: higher affinity than Hb; monomer with 1 heme
  • Dissolved (minor) — Henry's law: concentration = pressure × solubility; 0.3 mL O2/100 mL, not adequate for tissue demand
O2-Hb dissociation curve — sigmoidal
  • Lung PO2 = 100 mm Hg, saturation = 97.5%; a small drop in alveolar PO2 still allows adequate saturation
  • The steep portion lets tissue extract large amounts of O2 with a relatively small drop in PO2
  • Right shift: ↓ affinity, ↑ unloading — ↓ pH (↑ H+), ↑ temperature, ↑ PCO2, ↑ 2,3-BPG; exercise
  • Left shift: ↑ affinity, ↓ unloading — ↑ pH (↓ H+), ↓ temperature, ↓ PCO2, ↓ 2,3-BPG; pregnancy (fetal Hb has ↑ O2 affinity)

blocks.alt: Oxygen binding curves for myoglobin, normal Hb, 50% CO-Hb and anemia
blocks.cap: O2 content curves: myoglobin saturates at very low PO2; anemia (50% Hb) halves capacity but keeps the shape; 50% CO-Hb both halves capacity and shifts the curve left.

blocks.html:
Carbon dioxide transport
  • Bicarbonate (70%) — HCO3- diffuses into plasma; Cl- enters the RBC to maintain electroneutrality (chloride shift)
  • Bound to Hb (20%) — in the RBC, H+ binds deoxygenated Hb (HHb), which binds CO2 → carbamino-Hb
  • Dissolved (10%) — Henry's law; CO2 is 20× more soluble in blood than O2

blocks.alt: CO2 transport in the red blood cell
blocks.cap: CO2 from tissue: most is converted by carbonic anhydrase to H+ + HCO3- (HCO3- exits in exchange for Cl-), some binds Hb, a little stays dissolved.

blocks.html:
Hypoxia vs hypoxemia
  • Hypoxia — ↓ O2 delivery to tissues; SpO2 = 88-92% (normal SpO2 = 95+%)
  • Hypoxemia — ↓ PaO2 (< 80 mm Hg), insufficient oxygenation of blood; O2 is not reaching the alveoli or not diffusing from alveoli to blood
  • Hyperventilation = low PaCO2; hypoventilation = high PaCO2

blocks.html:
Compensation rules
  • The body never overcompensates
  • Lungs compensate faster (5-10 min) than kidneys (24 h)
  • SMORE (compare PaCO2 and pH): same direction = metabolic, opposite direction = respiratory

blocks.html:
Regulation of respiration

Spontaneous respiration comes from rhythmic discharges of the motor neurons to the respiratory muscles.

  • Voluntary control — influences ventilation within limits: cerebral cortex → corticospinal tract → spinal neurons
  • Automatic control — keeps blood PO2 and PCO2 in the normal range; three parts:

1. Respiratory muscles — receive impulses from the controller

2. Central controller — coordinates and responds to receptor input

  • Inspiratory area: dorsal medulla; inspiratory drive — inherent rhythmic excitability
  • Pneumotaxic center: pons; limits the duration of the inspiratory drive — inhibits inspiration
  • Apneustic center: lower pons; prevents termination of the inspiratory drive — stimulates inspiration
  • Expiratory area: ventral medulla; dormant during quiet breathing — forced expiration

3. Receptors — report blood gases and other factors

  • Central chemoreceptors: medulla; respond to blood PCO2 (via change in H+)
  • Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid and aortic bodies; respond to blood PO2 (< 60 mm Hg = ↑ RR and VT)
  • Lung receptors: pulmonary stretch (overdistention = ↓ RR), irritant (dust, cigarette smoke)
  • Other: nose and upper airway (chemical, mechanical), joint and muscle (exercise), pain and temperature
Responses
  • Responses to PaCO2 are rapid and sensitive — ↑ PaCO2 = ↑ ventilation; ↓ PaCO2 = ↓ ventilation
  • Responses to PaO2 are less marked — important at high altitude and in certain clinical conditions
  • Combined PaCO2 + PaO2 changes can exceed the sum of the individual responses
  • During exercise, arterial PCO2, PO2 and pH stay relatively constant

lectures.title: Obstructive and Restrictive Lung Disease
lectures.framing: A disease-by-disease comparison of the obstructive lungs (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma, bronchiectasis, CF) and the restrictive ones (IPF, sarcoidosis, GPA, ARDS, neuromuscular and chest wall). Read each column the same way — cause → pathology → presentation → diagnosis → treatment → prognosis — and the discriminating feature usually sits in the pathology row.
lectures.keypoints: Pink puffer (emphysema) = matched V/Q, ↓ DLCO; blue bloater (chronic bronchitis) = V/Q mismatch, normal DLCO. Chronic bronchitis = productive cough > 3 months/year for > 2 consecutive years. Asthma is reversible (≥ 12% FEV1 rise after bronchodilator); bronchiectasis is irreversible dilation. CF sweat Cl- > 60 mmol/L (> 30 under 3 months), confirmed by a second sweat test + mutation analysis. IPF: corticosteroids are NOT effective — antifibrotics slow it. ARDS = PaO2/FIO2 < 300, not due to HF.

Asthma — diagnosis and control
  • Adults and children ≥ 6: spirometry showing reversible obstruction, or PEF variability, or a positive challenge test (see table)
  • Children 1-5: documented airflow obstruction + documented reversibility + no alternative diagnosis

blocks.cap: Children 1-5 years: diagnosis rests on documented obstruction and its reversibility (to SABA ± oral steroids, or a 3-month ICS trial), with no alternative diagnosis.

blocks.html:
Asthma predictive index — children 1-3 years
  • ≥ 4 wheezing episodes (> 24 h) in the past year, at least 1 physician-confirmed, + 1 major or 2 minor criteria
  • Major: parent with asthma; atopic dermatitis; allergic sensitization to ≥ 1 aeroallergen
  • Minor: wheezing apart from colds; eosinophilia (≥ 4%); allergic sensitization to milk, egg or peanuts
  • It is NOT a test for who has asthma now or who should be treated — it predicts who will keep wheezing into school age
Pediatric respiratory red flags
  • Symptoms before 6 months of age
  • Productive daily cough
  • No benefit from medications
  • Acute onset with no previous history
  • Stridor
  • Coughing with drinking/eating — risk of aspiration
  • Asymmetric sounds and imaging — foreign body
  • Family history of CF
  • Constitutional symptoms — failure to thrive, digital clubbing

Cystic fibrosis — mechanism

CFTR (ATP-gated Cl- channel) is defective, so mucus is dehydrated and cannot be cleared.

lectures.name: Respiratory Pharmacology
lectures.title: Other Common Respiratory Pathologies
lectures.framing: A tour of the conditions that round out respirology — hemoptysis, DVT/PE, mediastinal and pleural disease, atelectasis, pneumothorax and the Pancoast tumour. Two of them are algorithms worth knowing cold: hemoptysis (stabilize → investigate → treat the cause) and pleural effusion (Light's criteria split exudate from transudate).
lectures.keypoints: Hemoptysis: bleeding side DOWN, then find the source — bronchoscopy is the gold standard. The bronchial circulation is the high-pressure one. Light's criteria: fluid/serum protein > 0.5, fluid/serum LDH > 0.6, fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH → exudate. Tension pneumothorax: air enters but cannot exit → needle decompression. Mesothelioma = asbestos, not smoking. Anterior mediastinal masses = 5 Ts. Pancoast tumour → Horner syndrome, hoarseness, SVC syndrome.

blocks.html:
Approach to hemoptysis
  • Amount/rate is variable: 100-650 mL over 24 hours; massive = 100 cc/hour
  • Pulmonary artery circulation = low-pressure — supplies lung parenchyma
  • Bronchial artery circulation = high-pressure — supplies bronchi and visceral pleura

1. Stabilize the patient — vitals, IV access, group and screen; reverse anticoagulation (tranexamic acid)

  • Position lateral decubitus, bleeding side down
  • Endotracheal tube to place an endobronchial blocker; ventilate the elevated side
  • Control bleeding with argon plasma coagulation or catheter embolization

2. Investigate the cause — CXR, chest CT, arteriography, bronchoscopy = gold standard (direct visualization, sampling, biopsy)

3. Treat the cause — see table

blocks.html:
Mediastinum and pleura
  • Anterior mediastinal masses — 5 Ts: thyroid, thymus, thoracic aorta, terrible lymphoma, teratoma and germ cell tumours
  • Mesothelioma — cancer of the mesothelium lining the lungs; may cause hemorrhagic pleural effusion or pleural thickening; associated with inhaled asbestos; tobacco smoking is NOT a risk factor
Atelectasis — alveolar collapse

rows: Airway obstruction stops new air reaching distal airways

blocks.html:
Pleural effusion — excess fluid in the pleural space
  • Light's criteria: pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5; pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6; pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH
  • Exudate: cloudy (cellular) — infection, malignancy, connective tissue disease, lymphatic, trauma
  • Transudate: clear (hypocellular) — ↑ hydrostatic pressure (HF, Na+ retention), ↓ oncotic pressure (cirrhosis)

lectures.name: Gas Exchange and Hypoxia
lectures.title: Structure and Function of the Lung — Gas Exchange
lectures.framing: Gas exchange happens across the thin, vast blood-gas barrier, and Fick's law says what speeds or slows it. The clinical tool that falls out of this is the A-a gradient: it tells you whether hypoxemia comes from too little O2 reaching the alveoli (normal gradient) or O2 failing to cross into blood (increased gradient).
lectures.keypoints: PIO2 = FIO2 × (Patm − PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) = 150 mm Hg. PAO2 = PIO2 − PaCO2/0.8. Normal A-a gradient = (age/4) + 4. Normal gradient: high altitude, hypoventilation. Increased gradient: shunt, V/Q mismatch, diffusion impairment. Diffusion is fast with large area, large gradient and a thin interface — emphysema cuts area, fibrosis and pneumonia thicken the barrier. Hypoxic vasoconstriction can lead to pulmonary hypertension.

blocks.html:
Airway structure
  • Gas exchange takes place at the blood-gas barrier (BGB) in the alveoli — large area, thin interface
  • 23 generations of airway branching
  • Large airways: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi
  • Conducting zone: trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles; pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells; NO gas exchange — anatomic dead space; warms and humidifies air
  • Respiratory zone (acinus): respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs; cuboidal cells, simple squamous cells
  • Right lung = 3 lobes; more common site for inhaled foreign bodies (R main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical)
  • Left lung = 2 lobes; lingula (homolog of R middle lobe)

blocks.alt: Respiratory tract anatomy and bronchial tree
blocks.cap: Airway tree: trachea → main (primary) → lobar (secondary) → segmental (tertiary) bronchi.

blocks.html:
Alveolar cells
  • Type I pneumocytes — squamous; 97% of alveolar surface; thinly line the alveoli for optimal gas exchange
  • Type II pneumocytes — cuboidal, clustered; stem cell precursors for type I and II (proliferate after lung damage); secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies
  • Alveolar macrophages — phagocytose foreign material
Circulation and pleura
  • Pulmonary artery branches into a dense capillary network wrapped around the alveoli; in the capillaries blood sees the largest surface area and lowest velocity
  • Intrapleural space: between lung and chest wall; negative pressure (-5 mm Hg) from elastic properties — lungs tend to collapse inward, chest wall to spring outward
  • Pressure becomes atmospheric if a pneumothorax (hole in the diaphragm) is created — the lung collapses

Diffusion — Fick's law

V_gas = (A / T) × D × (P1 − P2) — A = area, T = thickness, D = diffusion constant, P1 − P2 = partial pressure gradient

  • Fast: large area, large pressure gradient, thin interface
  • Slow: small area (emphysema), small gradient, thick interface (pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis)
Partial pressures
  • Partial pressure = pressure exerted by one gas in a mixture = total pressure × fractional concentration
  • Partial pressure of a gas in solution = partial pressure of the gas in equilibrium with that solution
  • Inspired PO2: PIO2 = FIO2 × (Patm − PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) = 150 mm Hg (FIO2 = 21%; sea-level pressure = 760 mm Hg; water-saturated air = 47 mm Hg)
  • PAO2 = alveolar partial pressure of O2; PaO2 = arterial partial pressure of O2
  • PACO2 = PaCO2; normal = 40 mm Hg
  • Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = PIO2 − (PaCO2 / 0.8)
A-a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2
  • Difference between alveolar and arterial O2
  • Normal = (age/4) + 4; lower is better

lectures.title: Chest Radiology and Rhinology
lectures.framing: Two halves: a systematic CXR read (DRS. ABCDE) with the pattern of each common abnormality, and the rhinology comparison — allergic rhinitis, acute and chronic rhinosinusitis, epistaxis. The CXR half is about never skipping a zone; the rhinology half turns on duration (10 days, 4 weeks, 8-12 weeks).
lectures.keypoints: Do NOT miss: deviated trachea, pneumothorax, subdiaphragmatic free air. Adequate inspiration = anterior ribs 5-6 / posterior ribs 8-10 reach the diaphragm. Pulmonary edema = Kerley B-lines, peribronchial cuffing, cardiomegaly; LLL collapse = sail sign. Acute rhinosinusitis = 10+ days or double-worsening, < 4 weeks — watch and wait 7-10 days first; chronic = 8-12 weeks with endoscopic/CT evidence. Decongestants 3-7 days only (rhinitis medicamentosa). Anterior epistaxis (90%) comes from Kiesselbach's plexus; do NOT biopsy a juvenile nasal angiofibroma.

  • Breathing: lung field outlines, symmetry, pleura — do NOT miss pneumothorax

lectures.name: Pneumonia
lectures.title: Pneumonia, Tuberculosis and Upper Respiratory Infections
lectures.framing: Pneumonia = inflammation of the lung parenchyma with alveolar filling by exudate. The organising split is typical vs atypical vs hospital-acquired vs TB — but because typical and atypical are hard to tell apart clinically, empiric therapy covers both, chosen by the patient's comorbidities.
lectures.keypoints: CXR = gold standard for diagnosing and classifying pneumonia; atypicals do NOT show on Gram stain. Empiric CAP: no comorbidities → macrolide (azithromycin) + 3rd-gen cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) or doxycycline; elderly/comorbid → fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin). Hospital-acquired (Pseudomonas) → piperacillin/tazobactam + vancomycin. TB: 6 months INH + B6 + rifampin, plus pyrazinamide + ethambutol for the first 2; secondary TB favours the apices. PCP prophylaxis when CD4 < 200. Treat strep throat promptly to prevent rheumatic fever.

blocks.html:
Diagnosis — all pneumonia
  • Hx: host risk factors, travel, animal/environmental exposures
  • PEx: vitals, chest exam
  • Bloodwork: CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine
  • ABG: ↓ PaO2 (hypoxemia); normal or ↓ PaCO2 from tachypnea
  • CXR = gold standard — classifies the pneumonia
  • Sputum Gram stain and culture: identifies the pathogen; atypical organisms do NOT show up on Gram stain
  • CT thorax if worried about complications
Diagnosis — TB
  • Primary TB: PEx — fever, chest pain, otherwise normal
  • Secondary TB: cough (hemoptysis), weight loss, wasting, night sweats; crackles over affected area
  • TB skin test (PPD / Mantoux)
  • Organism culture for definitive diagnosis

Treatment

Bacterial and atypical etiologies are hard to differentiate, so start empiric therapy based on likely pathogens.

  • No comorbidities: macrolide (azithromycin) + 3rd-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone); doxycycline
  • Elderly and comorbid: fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin)
  • Hospital-acquired: piperacillin/tazobactam + vancomycin
  • Fungal: endemic mycoses — itraconazole or fluconazole; disseminated — amphotericin B and newer-generation azoles
  • HIV with CD4+ < 200 cells/mm3: prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP) — TMP-SMX, pentamidine, dapsone, atovaquone
  • Viral: supportive care; antivirals (oseltamivir, zanamivir) ↓ duration by 24 hours
Complications
  • Lung abscess — localized pus within the parenchyma; unresponsive to antibiotics
  • Empyema — pus in the pleural space; requires drainage

lectures.framing: Three kinds of lump, one question each time: benign or malignant, and what test decides it? For the lung, size and risk set the follow-up; for the thyroid, TSH decides the next test and ultrasound features decide the FNAB; for a lateral neck mass in an adult, assume cancer until proven otherwise.
lectures.keypoints: Mass > 3 cm; nodule < 3 cm; < 7 mm likely benign. Pleural or pericardial effusion = stage IV. Lung cancer: stage I-II resect or radiate, III chemoradiation, IV palliative. Thyroid nodules: 50% incidence, only 5% malignant; papillary and follicular raise thyroglobulin, medullary raises calcitonin. Rule of 7s (7 days infection, 7 months neoplasm, 7 years congenital) and the 80% rule for lateral neck masses. Salivary tumours: the smaller the gland, the more likely malignant. HPV-16 → oropharyngeal SCC with good prognosis.

Adult head and neck masses
  • Normal neck structures that feel like masses: submandibular gland, C2 transverse process, carotid bulb, sternocleidomastoid, hyoid bone, cervical rib
  • DDx (CITTENS): congenital, infectious, toxins, trauma, endocrine, neoplasms, systemic

blocks.html:
Rules for lateral neck masses
  • Rule of 7s: 7 days = infection; 7 weeks/months = neoplasm; 7 years = congenital
  • 80% rule: 80% neoplastic → 80% of those malignant → 80% metastatic → 80% from a primary H&N site
  • Age rule: < 16 years = congenital; > 40 years = neoplastic
  • Age + 80% rule: in an elderly patient, a lateral neck mass is cancer until proven otherwise
Workup
  • Hx: mass characteristics, recent H&N infections, exposures (animals, travel), skin cancer, dental work, smoking/EtOH, radiation, FHx, immunodeficiency, age
  • PEx: look for the primary, palpate where possible, cervical lymph node exam — lower lymph node = worse
  • Ix: labs, nasal endoscopy, ultrasound, FNAB, CT/MRI, open neck biopsy (lymphoma), panendoscopy (primary site)

blocks.title: Lateral neck mass in an older adult
blocks.html: By the age rule and the 80% rule, a lateral neck mass in an elderly patient is cancer until proven otherwise — usually a metastasis from a head and neck primary.

blocks.html:
Salivary gland disorders

Functional problems — hypersecretion (rare), drooling, dry mouth (common); treat the underlying cause

Sialolithiasis (stones) — submandibular gland

  • Pain, swelling; salivary colic (worse with meals)
  • Dx: palpation, sialography (submandibular = radiopaque, parotid = radiolucent), ultrasound, CT, sialendoscopy (rare)
  • Complications: fistula, acute suppurative sialadenitis, ductal stricture
  • Tx: gland massage, bimanual stone expression, hydration, sialagogues, antibiotics, surgical excision

Sialadenitis (infection) — bacterial (S. aureus), viral (HIV, mumps, coxsackie, influenza)

  • Risk factors: dehydration, post-surgery, Sjögren's syndrome (autoimmune)
  • Pain, swelling, induration, warmth, purulence at the ductal orifice, tender
  • Complications: fistula, abscess, deep neck space infection
  • Tx: gland massage, warm compress, hydration, sialagogues, antibiotics; reassess for complications in 3 days

Salivary gland tumours

  • Risk factors: radiation (7-30 year latency); NOT associated with smoking/EtOH, EXCEPT Warthin's
  • Larger gland = more likely benign; smaller gland = more likely malignant
  • Usually a painless lump; abnormal growth, facial nerve weakness, overlying skin changes
  • Ix: complete Hx and PEx (skin cancer inspection, facial nerve assessment), ultrasound, CT, FNAB
  • Tx: surgical excision (diagnostic + therapeutic) — complete resection, preserve facial nerve; radiation

Head and neck cancers
  • Most skin cancers occur in the H&N; H&N cancer patients have the poorest health-related quality of life of all cancer patients
  • Non-melanoma skin cancers are the most common (1 in 6 Canadians)
  • Squamous cell carcinoma — epithelial lining of nose, paranasal sinuses, oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, esophagus, ear
  • Risk factors: smoking/EtOH, HPV-16 (oropharyngeal; base of tongue, tonsils), EBV (nasopharyngeal), sun, previous cancers, radiation, FHx, wood dust/heavy metals, immunosuppression
  • HPV-positive: younger, healthy, educated, high SES, many sexual partners, no smoking/EtOH, lower T-stage, good prognosis
  • PEx / red flags: persistent otalgia, unilateral otitis media with effusion, hearing loss, aural fullness, pulsatile tinnitus, recurrent epistaxis, unilateral nasal obstruction, persistent rhinorrhea/sinusitis, sore throat > 3 weeks, odynophagia, dysphagia, trismus, non-healing ulcers, halitosis, numbness over teeth, hemoptysis, leukoplakia, erythroplasia, hoarseness, throat pain, stridor, neurologic asymmetry, diplopia, mental status change, constitutional symptoms
  • Ix: flexible endoscopy, FNAB, tissue biopsy, CT/MRI, CT chest (staging), panendoscopy (primary site)
  • Tx: early — surgical excision, radiation; advanced — surgical excision + radiation, or chemotherapy + radiation

lectures.name: Pediatric Asthma
lectures.title: Asthma Drugs, Pediatric Airway and ENT, and Treatment Review
lectures.framing: The respiratory drug classes, organised by what they do to airway tone and inflammation (↑ cAMP to relax, block M3 to stop constriction, suppress inflammation), then the stepwise asthma plan by age. The rest of the page covers the pediatric airway and ENT problems (congenital neck masses, dysphagia, stridor, hoarseness, tonsils, croup, foreign bodies, head and neck infections) and closes with a treatment review across the block.
lectures.keypoints: ICS is 1st-line for asthma; never LABA monotherapy — always with ICS. SABA/LABA work through ↑ cAMP; methylxanthines and roflumilast stop its breakdown; ipratropium/tiotropium block M3. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index (CYP1A2). Rinse after ICS to prevent thrush. A spacer raises MDI deposition from 2-10% to 30%. Croup = subglottic (biphasic/inspiratory stridor, barking cough, steeple sign); the pediatric airway is narrowest at the cricoid. Esophageal dysphagia: solids only = mechanical, solids + liquids = motility. Lemierre's = Fusobacterium necrophorum jugular thrombophlebitis.

  • Most effective drugs: 1-5 μm diameter, moderate lipophilicity, low systemic activity, high therapeutic ratio

Using an inhaler with spacer + mouthpiece
  1. Open
  2. Shake
  3. Insert
  4. Press down
  5. Slow deep breath in, hold for 10 s
  6. If another puff is needed, wait 30 s and repeat steps 2-5
  7. Drink or brush teeth
Asthma exacerbation
  • Target SpO2 ≥ 90%; nebulizers (SABA, SAMA); oral steroids; monitor PEF for improvement
  • Avoid: NSAIDs, beta blockers, sedatives

blocks.title: Never LABA alone in asthma
blocks.html: LABA monotherapy is contraindicated in asthma — it must be combined with an ICS (as in Advair, Symbicort, Zenhale).

Congenital neck masses (> 50%) — present at birth, but may not present at birth

Branchial cleft cyst (17% of masses) — lateral

  • Embryological arches normally fuse, but can form cysts and sinuses
  • Second cleft (> 90% of branchial cleft anomalies); M:F
  • 80% present by age 5; recurrent neck swelling with URTI, recurrent discharge in the lower neck
  • Tx: surgical excision of sinus and tract (3% recurrence); 20% recurrence if prior partial excision or abscess drainage

Thyroglossal duct cyst (16% of masses; 70% of congenital cysts) — midline

  • Infrahyoid 65%; suprahyoid 20%; hyoid 15%
  • Presents around ages 3-5; enlarges after URTI
  • Elevates on tongue protrusion
  • Tx: cystectomy (20% recurrence); Sistrunk procedure (< 5% recurrence) — remove cyst, thyroglossal tract, middle of hyoid bone and base of tongue

Lymphatic vascular malformations

  • Most occur in the H&N; 60% present at birth, 90% by age 2
  • Macrocystic: spaces > 2 mL; microcystic: spaces < 2 mL
  • Dx: soft mass in the posterior triangle, may change size, compressive symptoms, prone to infection or trauma, fixed to deep tissues
  • Ix: ultrasound (superficial), CT (extent), MRI (multiplanar)
  • Tx: watch and wait (unlikely to resolve spontaneously); aspiration (symptom control); sclerotherapy; incomplete excision (15-50% recurrence); complete excision (10% recurrence)

Dysphagia
  • Dysphagia — subjective difficulty or abnormality of swallowing
  • Odynophagia — pain with swallowing
  • Globus sensation — functional esophageal disorder: sensation of a lump, retained bolus or tightness in the throat NOT due to a structural lesion, GERD, mucosal abnormality or motility disorder
Phases of swallowing
  1. Oral: preparatory (bolus formed, solids chewed); transit (tongue propels bolus to posterior oral cavity)
  2. Pharyngeal: peristalsis toward the UES; epiglottis deflects over the trachea, UES opens
  3. Esophageal: peristalsis toward the LES and into the stomach

Stridor — harsh sound from turbulent airflow
  • Inspiratory = supraglottic, glottic
  • Expiratory = lower airway
  • Biphasic = subglottic
  • Surgical airway: cricothyrotomy through the cricothyroid membrane; tracheostomy below the cricoid cartilage
Hoarseness — workup
  • Hx: age, occupation, voice use/abuse, character of hoarseness, risk factors (cancer, trauma, surgery), other ENT issues, systemic symptoms (weight loss, fever, sore throat)
  • PEx: look, listen, feel

rows: Nodule, Reinke's edema, muscle tension dysphonia
Watch and wait, speech therapy, medialization, injection laryngoplasty
blocks.lead: Hoarseness — red flags: persistent (> 2 weeks) or progressive, positive risk factors, associated symptoms (dysphagia, otalgia, stridor)

rows: Entirely within the tonsillar pillar, or removed

blocks.html:
Tonsillitis — workup
  • Hx: tonsil size, redness, exudate, lymphadenopathy, exposures (previous infections and swabs), vaccinations
  • PEx: trismus, reduced ROM, tonsil grade, size/exudate/cervical nodes
  • Red flags: peritonsillar swelling, uvula deviation (peritonsillar abscess), trismus, restricted neck range (deep neck infection)
  • Ix: CBC + diff, serology, tumour markers, TSH; CXR, CT, ultrasound
  • Tx: watch and wait (48-72 h); antibiotics (amoxicillin + clavulanic acid); incision and drainage; tonsillectomy (bacterial)
Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy
  • 7 episodes in 1 year, 5/year for 2 years, or 3/year for 3 years
  • Other indications: obstructive sleep apnea, malignancy, ADD, peritonsillar abscess, tonsil stones, chronic tonsillitis, halitosis

Pediatric upper airway
  • Tongue larger in proportion to the mouth
  • Pharynx smaller
  • Epiglottis larger and floppier
  • Larynx anterior and superior (C4 → C6/7 with growth) — protects the airway
  • Narrowest at the cricoid (complete ring, no room to expand) — in adults, narrowest at the vocal folds
  • Trachea narrow and less rigid
Laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) — subglottic obstruction
  • Most common cause of stridor
  • Viral — parainfluenza, RSV, influenza
  • Ages 6 months to 3 years; spring and fall
  • Low-grade fever, respiratory distress, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, barking cough, steeple sign on X-ray
  • Tx: hydration, cold humidification; steroids, nebulized epinephrine, intubation (rare)
Foreign body aspiration
  • History is most important
  • Most common at ages 1-3; boys > girls
  • Vegetable matter is the most common object; if there is one foreign body, check for more
  • Ix: inspiratory/expiratory CXR (air trapping in the affected lung); lateral decubitus film (uncooperative children)
  • Tx: retrieval in a controlled setting in the OR — laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy

Deep neck space infections
  • Arise from a bacterial focus — teeth, tonsils, parotid, deep cervical nodes, middle ear, sinuses
  • Ix: CT
  • Tx: systemic antibiotics — ceftriaxone + flagyl, + vancomycin (MRSA risk factors), + piperacillin/tazobactam (pseudomonas coverage); incision and drainage
Lemierre's syndrome — infectious thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein (Fusobacterium necrophorum)
  • Pharyngitis, then fever < 1 week later, chills, rigors, toxic appearance; induration along the internal jugular vein
  • Ix: CT with contrast
  • Tx: ceftriaxone + flagyl, anticoagulation, drain local abscesses
  • Complications: septic emboli to the lungs, intravascular access
Mucormycosis — angio-invasive fungal infection, high mortality; respiratory or skin presentation
  • Rapid-onset fever, sinus pain, headache, nasal discharge; necrotic palate
  • Risk factors: severe immunocompromise, diabetes, steroids, iron chelator (deferoxamine)
  • Tx: IV amphotericin B, surgical debridement
